This does not eliminate all loss, because you still paid for the put and may have downside from your stock entry to the put strike, but it limits the damage below the strike.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body:
A protective put fits when you want to keep the stock but fear a near-term drawdown. It can make sense before earnings, during macro stress, after a large unrealized gain, or when tax/portfolio reasons make selling shares unattractive.

Example: you own 100 shares at $100 and buy a 95 put for $3. If the stock falls to $80 at expiration, the shares lose $2,000, but the put is worth $15, or $1,500. Net loss is about $500 plus the $300 premium cost already included in the put economics, so the protection materially reduces the drawdown. If the stock rallies to $115, you keep the upside but your net gain is reduced by the $300 insurance cost.

sections.heading: Cost and break-even
sections.body:
The put premium raises your effective break-even. If you buy stock at $100 and pay $3 for a protective put, your upside break-even becomes about $103 before commissions and fees. The stock must rise enough to cover the cost of insurance.

This is why protective puts should not be treated as free safety. If you repeatedly buy puts and the stock does not fall, the insurance cost can reduce returns. The question is whether the protection is worth the premium for the risk period you are trying to cover.

sections.heading: Choosing the put strike
sections.body:
A closer-to-the-money put protects sooner but costs more. A farther OTM put costs less but only helps after a larger drop. If you buy a 98 put on a $100 stock, protection begins quickly but the premium may be expensive. If you buy an 85 put, it may be cheap but does little for the first 15% decline.

Choose the strike based on the drawdown you can tolerate. If you cannot tolerate more than a 5-7% loss, a far OTM put is not enough protection. If you only want disaster insurance, a farther OTM put may be acceptable.

sections.heading: Alternatives
sections.body: Sometimes reducing share size is better than buying a put. Selling half the position reduces risk without paying premium. A collar can also finance part of the put by selling a call, but that caps upside. The best choice depends on whether you want to keep full upside, reduce capital at risk, or define a floor at the lowest possible cost.

key_points: A protective put is insurance for long stock.
The put creates a downside floor below the strike, minus premium cost.
Closer puts protect sooner but cost more; farther OTM puts are cheaper but protect later.
Insurance has a cost: break-even moves up by the premium paid.
Reducing shares or using a collar may sometimes be better than buying puts.
lessons.practice: Load the protective put template in Strategy payoff lab. Test stock down 5%, down 15%, flat, and up 15%. Then change the put strike from near-the-money to far OTM and compare protection versus premium cost.

lessons.title: Covered call
objectives: Generate income on stock you are willing to sell higher.
Understand capped upside, partial downside offset, and assignment risk.
Choose call strikes based on income goal, upside willingness, IV, and stock thesis.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body:
A covered call combines long stock with a short call. You must own at least 100 shares for each call contract sold. The shares cover the obligation because if the call is assigned, you can deliver the shares you already own.

You collect premium upfront. In exchange, you agree to sell the shares at the call strike if assigned. This means the premium gives income and a small downside cushion, but your upside is capped above the strike.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body:
A covered call fits when you are neutral to mildly bullish and willing to sell the shares at the strike. It can be useful when the stock has rallied near resistance, IV is elevated, or you want to generate income while holding shares.

Example: you own 100 shares at $100. You sell a 110 call for $3. If the stock stays below $110, you keep the premium. If the stock rises above $110 and you are assigned, you sell shares at $110 and keep the $3 premium. Your effective sale outcome is about $113 before fees. That is attractive only if you are truly willing to sell near that level.

sections.heading: Risk and reward
sections.body:
Maximum upside is capped. If you bought shares at $100 and sold the 110 call for $3, the best outcome at expiration is roughly $13 per share: $10 stock gain plus $3 premium. If the stock goes to $130, you still only participate up to the covered-call cap if assigned.

Downside risk remains substantial. If the stock falls from $100 to $80, the $3 premium only offsets part of the $20 stock loss. Covered calls are not true protection; they are income plus a small buffer.

sections.heading: Choosing the strike
sections.body:
A closer call strike pays more premium but caps upside sooner. A farther OTM call pays less premium but gives the stock more room to rally. Choose the strike based on where you would be comfortable selling shares.

Example: with stock at $100, selling the 105 call may pay $4 but caps upside quickly. Selling the 115 call may pay $1.25 but leaves more room. If your thesis is strong upside, do not sell a tight call just because the premium looks attractive.

sections.heading: Assignment and dividends
sections.body:
Covered calls can be assigned before expiration, especially if the call is in the money and an ex-dividend date is near. Assignment is not necessarily bad if you wanted to sell shares, but it is bad if you were trying to keep them.

Before selling a call, check earnings dates, dividend dates, and whether the strike matches your planned exit. If you would be upset selling shares at the strike, the call is too low or the strategy does not fit.

key_points: Covered calls generate premium but cap upside.
The strategy fits only if you are willing to sell shares at the strike.
Premium provides partial downside offset, not full protection.
Closer strikes pay more but cap upside sooner.
Assignment risk matters around dividends and deep ITM short calls.
lessons.practice: Try the covered call template. Test stock below entry, flat, slightly above the call strike, and far above the call strike. Write the stock gain/loss, premium kept, capped upside, and whether assignment would be acceptable.

lessons.title: Cash-secured put
objectives: Get paid to wait for a lower stock entry price.
Understand assignment, effective purchase price, and downside risk.
Use cash-secured puts only when ownership at the strike is acceptable.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body:
A cash-secured put means you sell a put and reserve enough cash to buy the shares if assigned. One standard put contract can obligate you to buy 100 shares at the strike. The cash reserve is usually strike x 100 shares minus premium received, depending on broker treatment.

You collect premium upfront. If the stock stays above the strike through expiration, the put may expire worthless and you keep the premium. If the stock falls below the strike, you may be assigned and buy shares at the strike.

sections.heading: Risk
sections.body:
The main risk is that the stock falls far below the strike. Your effective purchase price is strike minus premium received, but that does not protect you from a large decline.

Example: stock is at $100. You sell a 95 put for $2.50. If assigned, your effective stock cost is $92.50 before fees. That sounds attractive if you wanted to own the stock lower. But if the stock falls to $70, you still bought at an effective $92.50 and have a large unrealized loss. The premium helps, but it does not eliminate downside.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body:
A cash-secured put fits when you are willing to own the stock at the strike and you believe the downside risk is acceptable. It is often used by investors who want a lower entry price or by traders who expect the stock to stay above support.

Example: a stock you like trades at $100, and you would be happy owning it at $95. Selling the 95 put for $2.50 means you either keep the premium if the stock stays above $95, or you may buy the stock at an effective $92.50. This is a plan only if you truly want the shares at that level.

sections.heading: Choosing the strike
sections.body:
A closer strike pays more premium but has higher assignment probability. A farther OTM strike pays less premium but gives more cushion. Selling a very low-probability put for tiny credit may not be worth the tail risk.

Compare the credit to the capital at risk. If you collect $0.50 on a 90 put, you receive $50 but may be obligated to buy $9,000 of stock. That may be acceptable for high-quality names you want to own, but it is not free income.

sections.heading: Management
sections.body: If the put loses value quickly, some traders buy it back to lock in most of the profit rather than wait for expiration. If the stock falls toward the strike, decide whether you still want assignment. Rolling can delay assignment, but it can also hide a losing thesis. Do not roll only to avoid admitting the trade is wrong.

key_points: A cash-secured put is a short put backed by cash for possible assignment.
Effective purchase price is strike minus premium received.
Premium is income only if the downside and assignment risk are acceptable.
Closer strikes pay more but are more likely to be assigned.
Only sell puts on names you want to own at the strike.
lessons.practice: Model a cash-secured put at three strikes: near the money, 5% OTM, and 10% OTM. Compare credit, effective purchase price, max capital required, and loss if the stock falls 20%.

lessons.title: Vertical credit spreads
objectives: Earn premium with capped risk.
Understand max gain, max loss, break-even, and probability trade-offs.
Use credit spreads when direction and volatility assumptions support defined-risk premium selling.

sections.heading: Bull put spread
sections.body:
A bull put spread sells a put at a higher strike and buys a put at a lower strike with the same expiration. It is bullish to neutral because it profits if the stock stays above the short put strike. The long lower-strike put defines the risk.

Example: stock is at $100. Sell the 95 put for $2.00 and buy the 90 put for $0.75. Net credit is $1.25, or $125 per spread. Spread width is $5. Max gain is the $125 credit. Max loss is $5.00 - $1.25 = $3.75, or $375 per spread before fees. Break-even is short strike minus credit: $95 - $1.25 = $93.75.

sections.heading: Bear call spread
sections.body:
A bear call spread sells a call at a lower strike and buys a call at a higher strike with the same expiration. It is bearish to neutral because it profits if the stock stays below the short call strike. The long higher-strike call defines the risk.

Example: stock is at $100. Sell the 105 call for $2.10 and buy the 110 call for $0.90. Net credit is $1.20, or $120 per spread. Max gain is $120. Max loss is $5.00 - $1.20 = $3.80, or $380. Break-even is short strike plus credit: $105 + $1.20 = $106.20.

sections.heading: When credit spreads fit
sections.body:
Credit spreads can fit when IV is elevated, you expect price to stay above or below a level, and you want defined risk instead of naked short options. They are not pure direction trades; they combine direction, time decay, volatility, and probability.

A bull put spread may fit near support in a neutral-to-bullish regime. A bear call spread may fit near resistance in a neutral-to-bearish regime. In both cases, the short strike should be placed where your thesis says price is unlikely to finish.

sections.heading: Risk and management
sections.body:
Credit spreads have capped risk, but losses can still be larger than the credit received. A common mistake is focusing on high win rate while ignoring loss size. If you collect $1 and risk $4, one full loss can erase several winners.

Many traders close credit spreads after capturing 50-80% of max profit instead of waiting for expiration. This reduces gamma and assignment risk near expiration. If the short strike is threatened, decide whether to close, adjust, or accept the defined loss. Do not add size just because the spread moved against you.

key_points: Max gain is the net credit received.
Max loss is spread width minus credit.
Bull put spreads express bullish/neutral views; bear call spreads express bearish/neutral views.
Short strike placement should match support, resistance, probability, and premium.
Close winners before expiration; max profit is not required for a successful trade.
lessons.practice: Build a bull put spread and a bear call spread in Strategy payoff lab. For each, calculate max gain, max loss, break-even, and what stock price would invalidate the thesis.

lessons.title: Iron condor
objectives: Profit from range-bound prices with defined risk.
Understand short strikes, long wings, max profit, max loss, and break-even zones.
Use iron condors only when range, IV, and risk/reward assumptions are clear.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body:
An iron condor combines two credit spreads: a bull put spread below the market and a bear call spread above the market. You sell an OTM put spread and sell an OTM call spread at the same expiration. The short put and short call define the profit zone; the long put and long call define the maximum risk.

The trade profits most if the stock finishes between the two short strikes at expiration. In that case, all options can expire worthless and you keep the net credit. If price moves beyond either side, losses begin. The long wings cap the damage.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body:
An iron condor fits when you expect the stock to stay inside a range and IV is high enough to pay a reasonable credit. It is often used after a volatility spike, before a period of expected consolidation, or when support/resistance levels are well-defined.

Example: stock is at $100. You sell the 90/85 put spread and the 110/115 call spread for a combined $2.00 credit. The ideal outcome is the stock finishing between $90 and $110. Max gain is $200 per condor. If each spread is $5 wide, max loss is $5 - $2 = $3, or $300 per condor before fees.

sections.heading: Break-even zones
sections.body:
The lower break-even is the short put strike minus the total credit. The upper break-even is the short call strike plus the total credit. Using the example above, lower break-even is $90 - $2 = $88. Upper break-even is $110 + $2 = $112.

Between $90 and $110, the trade can keep full credit at expiration. Between $88 and $90 or $110 and $112, the trade may still be profitable but less than max profit. Outside $88 or $112, the trade loses money at expiration.

sections.heading: Risk and management
sections.body:
Iron condors can look attractive because they often have a wide profit zone, but the loss can be larger than the credit. A $2 credit on a $5-wide condor risks $3 to make $2. If the stock trends strongly, a condor can lose quickly.

Many traders manage condors before expiration. They may close at 50-75% of max profit, adjust the tested side, or close the trade if price breaks the expected range. Holding to expiration increases gamma and assignment risk, especially near the short strikes.

sections.heading: Common mistake
sections.body: The common mistake is selling condors only because IV is high without asking why IV is high. If a major event is coming, the market may be pricing a large move for a reason. A condor before earnings is not automatically safe just because the short strikes are far away. Compare the credit received with the expected move and the stock's historical event behavior.

key_points: An iron condor sells a put spread below price and a call spread above price.
Max gain is the total credit received.
Max loss is spread width minus total credit, assuming both sides have equal width.
Best fit is range-bound price action with IV rich enough to justify the risk.
Max loss occurs outside the long strikes; know that dollar amount before entry.
lessons.practice: Use an iron condor template and write the short put strike, long put strike, short call strike, long call strike, total credit, max loss, lower break-even, and upper break-even. Then test prices inside the range and outside both wings.

lessons.title: Straddle and strangle
objectives: Trade expected large moves without picking direction.
Understand premium cost, break-even levels, theta, and IV crush.
Decide when a straddle or strangle is justified by expected movement.

sections.heading: Long straddle
sections.body:
A long straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike and expiration, usually near the current stock price. The trade does not require picking direction; it requires a large enough move in either direction to overcome the combined premium.

Example: stock is at $100. You buy the 100 call for $4 and the 100 put for $4. Total cost is $8, or $800 per straddle. Upper break-even is $108. Lower break-even is $92. At expiration, the stock must finish above $108 or below $92 for the trade to profit before fees.

The straddle benefits from a large move and can benefit from IV rising before the event. It is hurt by time decay and IV crush after the event.

sections.heading: Long strangle
sections.body:
A long strangle buys an OTM call and an OTM put with the same expiration. It is cheaper than a straddle because both options are out of the money, but it needs a larger move to profit at expiration.

Example: stock is at $100. You buy the 105 call for $2 and the 95 put for $2. Total cost is $4. Upper break-even is $109. Lower break-even is $91. The strangle costs less than the straddle, but the stock must move farther before either option has enough intrinsic value to overcome the premium.

sections.heading: When they fit
sections.body:
Long straddles and strangles fit when you expect a large move but are uncertain about direction. They can be used before earnings, regulatory decisions, macro events, or technical compression breakouts. They are most attractive when IV is not already pricing an excessive move.

Example: a stock has been compressing in a tight range, IV is low relative to history, and a catalyst is coming. A straddle may fit if you expect a move larger than the combined premium. If IV is already very high, the same straddle may be too expensive unless you expect an unusually large move.

sections.heading: Expected move test
sections.body:
The first question is whether the expected move is larger than the premium paid. A simple approximation is the ATM straddle price. If a stock at $100 has an ATM straddle costing $8, the market is pricing roughly an 8% move by expiration.

If you buy that straddle, you need the actual move to beat the priced move, or you need IV to rise after entry. If the stock moves only 4%, the direction may look dramatic on the chart, but the straddle may still lose because the premium was too high.

sections.heading: Risk and management
sections.body:
Maximum loss for a long straddle or long strangle is the premium paid if both options expire worthless or lose most of their value. Because two options are purchased, theta can be heavy. After the expected event, IV can fall sharply, reducing both legs.

Some traders take profits before the event if IV rises and the position gains value. Others hold through the event only when they believe the move can exceed the priced move. If one side becomes profitable after a large move, management can include selling the winning leg, holding part of it, or closing the entire structure.

sections.heading: Straddle vs strangle choice
sections.body: Choose a straddle when you want more sensitivity near the current price and are willing to pay more. Choose a strangle when you want lower upfront cost and are willing to require a larger move. Straddles usually have higher delta/gamma sensitivity near the stock price. Strangles are cheaper but can decay quietly if the move is delayed or too small.

key_points: Long straddles buy a call and put at the same strike.
Long strangles buy an OTM call and OTM put.
Both need movement large enough to overcome total premium.
IV crush can hurt both legs after events.
Best when IV is relatively low before a known catalyst or when the expected move is underpriced.
lessons.practice: Use the long straddle template with before-expiration Greek mode. Test stock unchanged, +5%, -5%, +12%, and -12%. Then reduce IV by 10 vol points and observe whether the move still beats theta and IV crush.

lessons.title: Collar
objectives: Protect stock while financing part of the put with a short call.
Understand the floor, ceiling, net cost, and opportunity cost of a collar.
Know when a collar is better than selling shares or buying a protective put alone.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body:
A collar combines three pieces: long stock, long put, and short call. The long stock keeps ownership. The long put creates a downside floor. The short call helps pay for the put, but it creates an upside ceiling because shares may be called away at the call strike.

The result is a defined outcome range. Below the put strike, the put limits further downside. Above the call strike, upside is capped. Between the strikes, the position behaves mostly like stock, adjusted by the net option cost or credit.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body:
A collar fits when you own shares and want protection but do not want to sell the stock. It is common after a large gain, before earnings, during macro uncertainty, or when taxes/portfolio goals make selling unattractive.

Example: you own 100 shares at $100. You buy a 95 put for $3 and sell a 110 call for $2. The net option cost is $1. Your downside is cushioned below $95, but your upside is capped near $110. If the stock falls to $80, the put helps protect the position. If the stock rallies to $125, you likely give up upside above $110.

sections.heading: Net cost and zero-cost collars
sections.body:
The collar's net cost depends on the put premium minus the call premium. If the put costs more than the call credit, the collar is a debit. If the call credit fully pays for the put, it can be near zero cost. If the call credit exceeds the put cost, it can be opened for a small credit.

A zero-cost collar is not free in economic terms. You are paying by giving up upside above the short call strike. The question is whether that upside cap is acceptable in exchange for downside protection.

sections.heading: Choosing the strikes
sections.body:
The put strike determines how much downside you are willing to absorb before protection begins. A closer put protects sooner but costs more. A farther OTM put costs less but allows a larger drawdown.

The call strike determines how much upside you are willing to give away. A closer call funds more of the put but caps upside sooner. A farther OTM call gives more upside room but funds less protection.

Example: with stock at $100, a 95/110 collar protects below $95 and caps above $110. A 90/105 collar protects later and caps sooner; it may be cheaper, but it gives worse upside and weaker protection. A 98/120 collar protects sooner and leaves more upside, but it likely costs more.

sections.heading: Risks and management
sections.body:
The biggest risk is opportunity cost. If the stock rallies sharply, the collar can underperform simply holding shares. There is also assignment risk on the short call, especially around ex-dividend dates if the call is in the money.

Management depends on the goal. If the stock drops, the put is doing its job; decide whether to keep the protection, take profits on the put, or unwind the stock. If the stock rallies toward the short call, decide whether you are comfortable selling shares, rolling the call up/out, or removing the collar.

key_points: A collar defines a downside floor and an upside ceiling.
The long put protects; the short call helps finance the put.
A zero-cost collar still has opportunity cost because upside is capped.
Put strike controls protection; call strike controls upside sacrifice.
Assignment risk matters when the short call is in the money, especially near dividends.
lessons.practice: Use the Collar template in Strategy payoff lab. Test stock down 20%, down 5%, flat, up 10%, and up 25%. Then move the put closer and the call farther away; compare protection cost, downside floor, and upside cap.

lessons.title: Diagonal call spread
objectives: Finance long-dated bullish exposure by selling shorter-dated calls.
Understand the difference between the long anchor leg and the short income leg.
Manage upside squeezes, flat markets, and thesis failures.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body:
A diagonal call spread buys a longer-dated call and sells a shorter-dated call, usually at a higher strike. The long call is the bullish anchor. The short call is the income leg that attempts to collect time decay. Because the options have different expirations and often different strikes, the position is called diagonal.

Example: stock is at $100. You buy a 90-day 95 call for $9 and sell a 30-day 110 call for $2. Your net debit is $7. The long call gives bullish exposure for several months. The short call brings in premium and reduces cost, but it caps or complicates upside during the short call's life.

sections.heading: Management
sections.body:
Management depends on price path.

If price is flat or rises slowly, the short call may decay faster than the long call. You can potentially buy it back cheaper or let it expire, then sell another short call if the bullish thesis remains.

If price rallies quickly toward or through the short call strike, the short leg becomes the problem. You may need to buy to close the short call, roll it up/out, or close the whole diagonal. Do not ignore the short call just because the long call is profitable; the short leg can cap gains and create assignment risk.

If price drops, the long call loses value and the short call may profit. Before selling another call, reassess whether the bullish thesis still exists. Repeatedly selling calls against a broken long call can turn a directional thesis into a slow bleed.

sections.heading: Why traders use diagonals
sections.body:
Diagonals try to combine long-term directional exposure with short-term income. The long call keeps upside exposure with less capital than stock. The short call attempts to harvest theta from nearer-term options.

This can fit when you are moderately bullish over several months but expect the stock to move gradually, not explode immediately. It can also fit when near-term IV is relatively high and longer-term IV is more reasonable.

sections.heading: Risk and reward
sections.body:
Maximum risk is generally close to the net debit paid if the structure is fully paid upfront, but real-world risk depends on assignment, early exercise, and how the short call is managed. Upside is not as simple as a normal debit spread because the long and short calls expire at different times.

Example: if you pay $7 net for the diagonal, your initial capital at risk is about $700 per spread. If the stock stays below the short call and the short call decays, you may reduce your cost basis by selling calls over time. If the stock gaps far above the short strike, the short call may lose quickly even though the long call gains.

sections.heading: Strike and expiration selection
sections.body:
The long call is often ITM or ATM with enough time for the thesis to develop. Higher delta on the long call gives more stock-like behavior. The short call is often OTM at a price where you are willing to cap near-term upside.

A shorter short-call expiration decays faster but requires more active management. A longer short-call expiration brings in more premium but caps upside for longer. The short strike should not be chosen only by premium; it should reflect where you believe the stock is unlikely to close before the short expiration.

key_points: The long call is the bullish anchor; the short call is the income/cost-reduction leg.
Flat or slow-up markets can help because the short call decays.
Fast rallies can create pressure because the short call caps or offsets gains.
Broken bullish thesis means stop reselling calls mechanically.
Short leg may require margin and assignment planning; check broker requirements.
lessons.practice: Build a diagonal with a 90 DTE long call and 30 DTE short call. Test three paths: flat, slow rally, and fast rally through the short strike. For each, write what you would do with the short call.

lessons.title: Stock plus bull call spread
objectives: Combine stock ownership with defined-risk option leverage.
Use a bull call spread as an upside accelerator without risking unlimited option losses.
Understand when adding a spread improves or overcomplicates a stock position.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body:
This structure combines long stock with a bull call spread. The stock is the core position and provides patient, linear exposure. The bull call spread is an added defined-risk upside layer: buy a lower-strike call and sell a higher-strike call with the same expiration.

The spread costs a net debit. Its maximum loss is the debit paid. Its maximum value at expiration is the spread width. The short call caps the spread's upside, but it also reduces the cost compared with buying a naked call.

sections.heading: Management
sections.body:
If price rallies hard, the bull call spread can approach its maximum value before expiration. Many traders close the spread after capturing most of its value, such as 70-90%, rather than waiting for the final dollars. You can keep the stock as the core holding and then decide whether to sell covered calls, add another spread, or simply hold.

If price is flat, the stock may hold value but the spread can decay. If price falls, the stock loses and the spread may also lose most of its debit. The spread is defined risk, but it does not hedge the stock; it adds bullish exposure.

sections.heading: Example
sections.body:
Suppose you own 100 shares at $100. You add a 100/110 bull call spread for a $4 debit. The spread can be worth up to $10 at expiration if the stock is at or above $110. Max profit on the spread is $6 per share, or $600 per spread, before fees. Max loss on the spread is the $400 debit.

If the stock rises to $112, the shares gain $1,200 and the spread can add up to about $600. If the stock stays at $100, the shares are flat but the spread can lose the $400 debit. If the stock falls to $90, the shares lose $1,000 and the spread likely loses most or all of its debit.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body:
This structure fits when you already want to own the stock but also see a defined upside catalyst. It can be useful when IV is reasonable and you want extra upside exposure without buying more shares.

Example: a stock is breaking out from a long base. You own shares for the longer-term thesis, but you expect a faster move over the next 30-60 days. A bull call spread can add efficient upside for that window while keeping the option risk limited.

sections.heading: When it does not fit
sections.body:
It may not fit if the stock thesis is slow, IV is very expensive, or the expected move is smaller than the spread's debit. It also may be unnecessary if your stock position is already large enough. Adding a spread increases bullish exposure; it is not protection.

A common mistake is adding option leverage after a stock has already made a large move and IV has expanded. In that case, the spread may have poor reward/risk unless another strong catalyst remains.

key_points: Stock provides patience; the bull call spread provides defined-risk upside acceleration.
The spread's max loss is the debit paid.
The spread's max value is the distance between strikes.
This structure adds bullish exposure; it does not hedge the stock.
Best fit is a stock you want to own plus a time-bound upside catalyst.
lessons.practice: Build stock plus a 100/110 bull call spread in the Custom strategy table. Test stock at 90, 100, 105, 110, and 120. Separate the stock P&L from the spread P&L and decide whether the added leverage was worth the debit.

lessons.title: LEAPS with short call
objectives: Use a long-dated call as a stock substitute with an income overlay.
Understand how short calls reduce cost but cap or complicate upside.
Manage LEAPS, short-call assignment risk, and thesis decay over time.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body:
This structure buys a long-dated call, often called a LEAPS, and sells shorter-dated calls against it. The LEAPS acts as a stock substitute because it provides bullish delta with less capital than buying 100 shares. The short calls attempt to collect premium over time.

Example: stock is at $100. Instead of buying 100 shares for $10,000, you buy a 12-month 80 call for $25, or $2,500. Then you sell a 30-day 110 call for $2, or $200. The short call reduces the net cost, but it creates a near-term cap and management obligation.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body:
This fits when you are bullish long term, want lower capital tie-up than stock, and are willing to actively manage short calls. It can work best when the long call has high delta, enough time, and reasonable IV, while short calls can be sold at strikes where you are comfortable reducing upside.

Example: you believe a stock can grind higher over the next year, but you do not want to commit the full cash required for shares. A deep ITM LEAPS may provide stock-like exposure. Selling monthly OTM calls can reduce cost if the stock rises slowly or stays range-bound.

sections.heading: How it differs from covered calls
sections.body:
A covered call uses stock as collateral for the short call. A LEAPS with short call uses a long call as the anchor. This is sometimes called a poor man's covered call, but it is not identical to a covered call.

The LEAPS can lose value from time decay and IV changes. It also may not perfectly cover assignment risk if the short call is exercised. Brokers may treat the structure differently for margin and exercise. Because the anchor is an option, not shares, management is more complex.

sections.heading: Choosing the LEAPS
sections.body:
Many traders prefer a LEAPS that is ITM with higher delta, such as 0.70-0.85, because it behaves more like stock. A low-delta OTM LEAPS is cheaper but may not provide stable exposure and can decay if the stock does not move.

The expiration should give the thesis enough time. A 12-24 month call has less daily theta pressure than a short-dated call, but it still loses time value if the thesis is delayed. IV matters too: buying LEAPS when IV is very high can create poor returns if IV normalizes.

sections.heading: Choosing the short call
sections.body:
The short call should usually be OTM and short-dated enough to decay faster than the LEAPS. Choose a strike where you are willing to cap near-term upside or roll if challenged. Selling calls too close to the stock price brings in more premium but increases the chance of capping a rally.

Example: stock at $100, long 80 LEAPS, sell the 110 call for 30 days. If the stock stays below $110, the short call may decay. If the stock rallies to $120 quickly, the short call becomes a problem and may need to be closed or rolled.

sections.heading: Risks and management
sections.body:
The biggest risks are fast upside moves, thesis failure, IV contraction, and poor rolling decisions. If the stock rallies sharply, the short call can offset gains on the LEAPS. If the stock falls, the LEAPS loses value and selling small calls may not repair the damage. If IV falls, the LEAPS can lose value even if the stock is flat or slightly up.

Management rules should be written before entry: when to close the short call, when to roll, when to stop selling calls, and when to exit the LEAPS. Do not sell short calls mechanically if the long-term bullish thesis has failed.

key_points: The LEAPS is the long-term bullish anchor; the short call is the income leg.
This is similar to a covered call but not identical because the anchor is an option, not shares.
Higher-delta LEAPS behave more like stock but cost more.
Short calls reduce cost but can cap or complicate upside.
LEAPS still suffer from IV and time if the thesis delays.
lessons.practice: Compare buying 100 shares with buying one high-delta LEAPS. Then add a short 30-day OTM call. Test flat, slow rally, fast rally, and decline scenarios. Write how the short call helps or hurts in each path.

lessons.title: Rolling covered calls
objectives: Adjust short calls when price approaches the strike.
Understand roll up, roll out, roll up-and-out, and when assignment is acceptable.
Roll only when the new trade improves the plan, not simply to avoid being wrong.

sections.heading: Roll up
sections.body:
Rolling up means buying back the current short call and selling a higher-strike call, usually in the same expiration. The goal is to recover more upside when the stock rises faster than expected.

Example: you own 100 shares at $100 and sold a 105 call for $2. The stock rallies to $104.50 and the call is now worth $3.50. You can buy to close the 105 call and sell a 110 call. If the 110 call pays enough premium, the roll may give the stock more upside room. If the new premium is too small, the roll may not be worth it.

Rolling up usually costs money or reduces credit because you are buying back a call that gained value and selling a farther OTM call with less premium. It makes sense only if you want to keep the shares and the higher strike improves the expected outcome.

sections.heading: Roll out
sections.body:
Rolling out means closing the current short call and selling a later-expiration call, often at the same strike. The goal is to collect more time premium when the stock is near the strike and you still believe the covered call plan makes sense.

Example: you sold a 105 call expiring this week. The stock is at $104.80 and assignment is possible. You buy to close the current 105 call and sell next month's 105 call for a larger credit. This can delay assignment and bring in more premium, but it also extends the obligation and keeps your upside capped for longer.

Rolling out is not automatically better. If you keep rolling the same strike, you may trap the stock under a ceiling and miss a larger trend.

sections.heading: Roll up and out
sections.body:
Rolling up and out means moving both the strike higher and the expiration later. This is common when the stock rallies and you want more upside room while still collecting enough premium to justify the adjustment.

Example: stock rallies through your 105 short call. You buy to close the 105 call and sell a 110 call expiring next month. The later expiration helps fund the higher strike. The trade-off is more time in the position and continued assignment risk.

A good roll up-and-out should answer: how much additional upside do I recover, how much extra premium do I receive or pay, how much longer am I obligated, and would I still be happy selling shares at the new strike?

sections.heading: When not to roll
sections.body:
Do not roll automatically. If assignment at the strike is acceptable, letting shares be called away may be the cleanest outcome. If rolling requires paying too much debit, extends the trade too far, or keeps you in a stock you no longer want, the roll may be a mistake.

Example: you bought shares at $90 and sold the 105 call because you were willing to exit at $105. The stock rallies to $108. Assignment would lock in a strong gain plus the premium. Rolling from fear of missing more upside may turn a successful planned exit into an unmanaged trade.

A roll should improve expected value. It should not be used only to avoid assignment, avoid taking a loss on the short call, or emotionally chase upside.

sections.heading: Covered call roll checklist
sections.body:
Before rolling, write the math: current short call value, new short call credit, net debit or credit of the roll, new strike, new expiration, added upside, and assignment risk. Then compare the roll with simply letting assignment happen.

If the new strike is still a price where you are willing to sell shares, the premium is reasonable, and the added time fits your thesis, rolling can be useful. If not, close the call, let assignment happen, or exit the stock.

key_points: Roll up to recover upside, but only if the cost is justified.
Roll out to collect more time premium, but it extends the obligation.
Roll up-and-out can balance higher strike and additional credit.
Let assignment happen when it matches the original plan.
Roll only if math improves expected outcome, not from fear alone.
lessons.practice: Paper-trade a covered call roll when stock reaches 90% of your short strike. Compare three choices: do nothing, roll up, and roll up-and-out. Write net debit/credit, new cap, added time, and whether assignment would actually be a bad outcome.

lessons.title: Managing diagonals
objectives: Protect the long-term thesis while actively managing the short leg.
Understand how flat, rally, and decline paths change diagonal management.
Avoid letting the short call damage the long call thesis during fast moves.

sections.heading: Flat market
sections.body:
A flat or slow-moving market is often the path a diagonal wants. The short option decays faster than the long option, allowing you to potentially buy it back cheaper or let it expire. If the long-term bullish thesis remains intact, you may sell another short call for the next cycle.

Example: stock is at $100. You own a 90-day 95 call and sold a 30-day 110 call. After two weeks, the stock is still near $100 and the short call has lost most of its value. You can buy it back for a small debit or let it expire, then sell another OTM call. This reduces the net cost of the long call over time.

sections.heading: Strong rally
sections.body:
A strong rally is where diagonals become difficult. The long call gains, but the short call can gain too and cap the position. If price moves quickly toward or through the short strike, the short call can become the risk-management priority.

Example: stock jumps from $100 to $113 and your short 110 call is now in the money. If you do nothing, the short call can offset much of the LEAPS/long-call gain and may create assignment risk. Possible actions include buying to close the short call, rolling it up/out, or closing the entire diagonal for a profit. The correct action depends on whether the long-term thesis improved and whether the roll math is favorable.

Do not sacrifice a good long call only to defend a short call that was meant to be temporary income.

sections.heading: Decline
sections.body:
If the stock declines, the short call may profit or expire worthless, but the long call loses value. The key question becomes whether the original bullish thesis is still valid. If the thesis is intact, you may sell another short call to reduce cost. If the thesis is broken, repeatedly selling calls can become a slow attempt to repair a bad long option.

Example: stock drops from $100 to $90 after weak news. The short 110 call is nearly worthless, but the long 95 call has lost value. If the chart and fundamentals are broken, closing the structure may be better than selling a lower short call. If the drop is a normal pullback into support, selling a new short call farther OTM may still fit.

sections.heading: Short leg rules
sections.body:
The short call is not the main thesis; it is an income tool. Define rules for it before entry. For example: close the short call if it reaches 2x the credit received, roll only for a net credit, avoid selling calls through earnings, or never sell a short call below a price where you would be unhappy capping upside.

Without rules, traders often sell short calls too aggressively, then spend the entire trade fighting the short leg instead of benefiting from the long leg.

sections.heading: Long leg rules
sections.body:
The long call is the anchor. Choose it with enough time and enough delta to support the thesis. If the long call loses too much delta or the thesis takes too long, the structure can become less effective. Decide in advance when the long leg should be closed, rolled farther out, or converted into another structure.

Example: if your long call has 90 DTE at entry, you may decide to reassess at 45 DTE. If the thesis has not developed, rolling the long call earlier may preserve optionality better than waiting until theta accelerates.

key_points: Flat markets can help diagonals because the short call decays faster.
Fast rallies require active short-call management.
Declines require reassessing whether the long-call thesis is still valid.
The short call is an income tool, not the main thesis.
Never defend the short leg by sacrificing the long leg.
lessons.practice: Before entering a diagonal, write your action for five scenarios: flat price, slow rally, fast rally through short strike, pullback to support, and thesis failure. Include when you would close, roll, or stop selling short calls.

lessons.title: Closing spreads at a profit
objectives: Bank gains without needing maximum theoretical profit.
Understand why gamma, assignment, and liquidity risk increase near expiration.
Use planned profit targets for credit and debit spreads.

sections.heading: Credit spreads
sections.body:
Credit spreads make money as the spread loses value. If you sold a spread for $1.00, the maximum possible profit is $100 per spread. But you do not need to hold to expiration to be successful. Many traders close credit spreads after capturing 50-80% of max profit.

Example: you sell a 95/90 put credit spread for $1.20. If the spread later trades for $0.30, you can buy it back and lock in $0.90, or $90 per spread before fees. That captures 75% of max profit and removes the remaining risk. Holding for the final $0.30 exposes you to gap risk, gamma risk, and possible assignment near expiration.

sections.heading: How to close
sections.body:
Close the spread as a single combo order when possible. For a credit spread, closing usually means buying back the short option and selling the long option in one order. This controls the net debit you pay to exit. Closing one leg at a time can leave temporary naked exposure.

Example: you sold the 95 put and bought the 90 put. To close, buy to close the 95 put and sell to close the 90 put as one vertical spread order. If you only buy back the short put and forget to sell the long put, you may leave unused value. If you only sell the long put first, you may temporarily hold a naked short put.

sections.heading: Debit spreads
sections.body:
Debit spreads make money as the spread gains value. If you bought a 100/110 call spread for $4, the maximum value is $10 and max profit is $6. Many traders close when the spread reaches 70-90% of max value instead of waiting for expiration.

Example: your $4 debit spread rises to $8.50. You could close for a $4.50 gain. Waiting for the final $1.50 of possible value may not be worth the risk of reversal, especially if expiration is near or the stock is close to the short strike.

sections.heading: Why not wait for max profit
sections.body:
Near expiration, option gamma rises and small stock moves can change spread value quickly. Assignment risk also becomes more relevant when short options are in the money. Liquidity can worsen near expiration or around events.

The last 10-20% of theoretical profit may carry more risk than it appears. A spread that is almost a winner can become a problem if the stock gaps through the short strike. Taking planned profits removes uncertainty and frees capital for better setups.

sections.heading: Loss management
sections.body:
Profit targets are only half of spread management. You also need a loss plan. Some traders close a credit spread if the loss reaches 1.5x or 2x the credit received, or if price breaks the technical level that justified the short strike. Others adjust only if the new risk/reward improves.

Example: you sold a put spread below support. If support breaks on heavy volume, the original thesis is invalid. Holding only because max loss is defined can still be poor management. Defined risk means the loss is capped, not that you must take the full loss.

key_points: Credit spreads can be closed after capturing 50-80% of max profit.
Debit spreads can be closed after reaching most of max value.
Use combo orders to avoid leaving one naked leg.
Near expiration, gamma and assignment risk can rise quickly.
Close the entire spread; do not leave one naked leg.
lessons.practice: Choose one credit spread and one debit spread. Calculate max profit, 70% profit target, max loss, and the price level that invalidates the trade. Write the exact closing order for each spread.

lessons.title: Margin on short options
objectives: Understand why short option legs tie up buying power.
Distinguish naked, covered, cash-secured, and defined-risk margin profiles.
Check buying-power impact before entry, not after a squeeze.

sections.heading: Naked short options
sections.body:
A naked short option is a short option without stock ownership, cash security, or a defined-risk long option leg. Naked shorts can require high margin because potential losses can be very large. A naked short call is especially dangerous because the stock can theoretically rise without limit.

Example: selling one naked 100 call for $2 brings in $200, but if the stock rises to $130, the option can be worth about $30, creating roughly a $2,800 loss before fees. The broker may increase margin requirements as the stock moves, which can force liquidation at the worst time.

Naked short options should be avoided unless the trader is experienced, capitalized, and intentionally accepting the risk.

sections.heading: Spreads and diagonals
sections.body:
Defined-risk spreads usually require less buying power because the long option caps the short option's risk. For example, a 100/105 call credit spread has a $5 width. If you collect $1 credit, max loss is about $4, or $400 per spread before fees. The broker can calculate the risk because the long call limits the damage.

Diagonals are more complicated because the long and short options have different expirations. A long-dated call may reduce risk, but it may not fully cover the short call in the broker's margin model. Some brokers require additional buying power for the short leg, especially if assignment or expiration mismatch creates risk. Always preview margin before sending the order.

sections.heading: Covered call
sections.body:
A covered call is usually lower margin because stock ownership covers the short call. If you own 100 shares and sell one call, assignment means you deliver shares you already own. The risk is not unlimited short-call risk; the risk is that your stock upside is capped and the stock can still fall.

Example: own 100 shares at $100, sell a 110 call. If assigned, you sell shares at $110. The broker sees the shares as covering the call. However, if you sell more calls than your shares cover, the extra calls are naked and can create major margin risk.

sections.heading: Cash-secured puts
sections.body:
A cash-secured put reserves cash to buy shares if assigned. If you sell one 95 put, the obligation is to buy 100 shares at $95, or $9,500 notional. The premium reduces effective cost but does not remove the capital requirement.

Example: sell a 95 put for $2.50. Effective purchase price if assigned is $92.50, but the broker may still reserve cash or buying power close to the strike value. This is safer than a naked put in a margin account because you are planning for assignment, but the stock can still fall below your effective cost.

sections.heading: Margin expansion risk
sections.body:
Margin is not always static. During volatility spikes, brokers can increase requirements. A position that looks acceptable in calm markets can consume much more buying power during stress. This is especially important for short options, concentrated positions, and multi-leg trades near expiration.

Example: you sell several credit spreads because each uses modest buying power. If volatility spikes and the spreads move against you, required buying power can increase while the account equity falls. This combination can create forced decisions. Keep extra liquidity instead of using every dollar of buying power.

sections.heading: Pre-entry margin checklist
sections.body: Before entering a short-option trade, check max loss, buying-power reduction, assignment obligation, whether the risk is defined, what happens if IV doubles, and whether the account could handle a gap against the position. If the trade only works when everything goes smoothly, it is too large or too fragile.

key_points: Naked short options can create large and changing margin requirements.
Defined-risk spreads usually reduce buying-power requirements because max loss is known.
Covered calls are covered only when share quantity matches short call quantity.
Cash-secured puts require cash readiness for assignment.
Keep liquidity buffer; do not use all buying power.
Check margin impact before entry, not after a squeeze.
lessons.practice: Build three examples in the strategy table: naked short call, defined-risk credit spread, and covered call. For each, write max loss, assignment obligation, buying-power impact, and what could happen if the stock gaps 15% against you.

lessons.title: Pre-trade questions
objectives: Force discipline before capital is at risk.
Convert a trade idea into a written plan with max loss, invalidation, and management rules.
Avoid trades where thesis, structure, size, or liquidity are unclear.

sections.heading: Checklist
sections.body:
A pre-trade checklist turns an opinion into a plan. Before entering, answer these questions clearly:

1. What is the market regime: risk-on, neutral, risk-off, or event-driven?
2. What is the stock thesis, and what would prove it wrong?
3. Is IV cheap, fair, expensive, or event-driven relative to this stock?
4. What structure fits the thesis: stock, long option, debit spread, credit spread, hedge, or no trade?
5. What is the max loss in dollars and as a percentage of the account?
6. What happens if price does nothing?
7. What happens if IV falls or rises sharply?
8. Is liquidity acceptable: bid/ask spread, volume, open interest?
9. What is the exit plan for profit, loss, and time decay?
10. Does the expiration match the expected timeline?

sections.heading: Example: long call checklist
sections.body:
Suppose you want to buy a call because a stock is breaking out. A good checklist answer might be: regime is risk-on, sector is leading, stock is above resistance, IV is low to medium, catalyst is within 30 days, and max loss is the premium paid. The invalidation is a close back below breakout support. If price does nothing for two weeks, exit because theta will accelerate.

A weak checklist answer would be: 'I think it goes up.' That is not enough. You need direction, timing, IV view, max loss, and invalidation.

sections.heading: Example: credit spread checklist
sections.body:
Suppose you want to sell a put credit spread. A good checklist answer might be: market is neutral to bullish, stock is above support at $95, IV is elevated, sell the 95/90 put spread for $1.20, max loss is $3.80 per share or $380 per spread, break-even is $93.80, and you will close at 70% of max profit or if support breaks.

The key is that the short strike should be placed for a reason. Selling a spread only because the credit looks attractive is not enough.

sections.heading: Position size question
sections.body:
Every checklist should translate risk into account impact. If max loss is $500 and your account is $25,000, the trade risks 2% of the account. If max loss is $2,500, it risks 10%, which may be too large even if the setup looks good.

Options can make small premiums look harmless, but spreads, assignment, and multiple contracts can create larger risk than expected. Always calculate total dollars, not only per-share premium.

sections.heading: When the checklist says wait
sections.body:
A checklist is useful because it sometimes tells you not to trade. If IV is expensive and you want to buy calls without a catalyst, wait. If bid/ask spread is wide, wait or choose a more liquid strike. If the max loss is too large, reduce size or skip. If the trade only works in one perfect scenario, it may be too fragile.

Waiting is not inactivity. Waiting is choosing not to accept low-quality risk.

key_points: A trade idea is not a plan until max loss, invalidation, and exit rules are defined.
Regime and IV should influence structure choice.
Liquidity matters; wide spreads can erase edge.
Position size must be based on total dollar risk.
If you cannot answer clearly, wait.
lessons.practice: Use the Pre-trade checklist page before every new options structure. Write answers for one long call, one credit spread, and one stock-plus-option structure. If any answer is vague, revise the trade or skip it.

strategy_playbook.name: Long call
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Best when the market is risk-on: index trend is improving, VIX is stable or falling, sector leadership supports the stock, and you expect a directional move within the option's life.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use a long call when you want bullish exposure with defined risk and less capital than buying shares. The setup should have a clear catalyst or technical trigger, because time decay works against you every day.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: stock is at $100, IV is low to medium, and a breakout above resistance could target $110 within 30-45 days. Buying a 100 call for $4 risks $400 per contract. Expiration break-even is $104. If the stock reaches $112 quickly, the call can gain from delta and gamma. If the stock stays near $100, the call can lose most or all of the premium.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid when IV is already inflated after a big move, when the thesis has no timing catalyst, or when the expected move is smaller than the premium hurdle.
strategy_playbook.management: Define the invalidation level before entry. Consider taking profits if the call captures a large portion of the expected move early. If the stock stalls and time decay accelerates, exit instead of hoping.
strategy_playbook.risks: Time decay and IV drop can hurt even if direction is right. Max loss is usually the premium paid.

strategy_playbook.name: Bull call spread
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Fits a bullish market where you expect upside, but you want lower cost than a naked long call or IV is not cheap enough to justify buying premium alone.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use when you have a realistic upside target. Buy the call near the price area you expect the stock to hold or break above, and sell a higher call near the target zone. This reduces debit but caps upside.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: stock is at $100 and your target is $110. Buy the 100 call for $5 and sell the 110 call for $2. Net debit is $3, or $300 per spread. Max value is $10, so max profit is $7, or $700. Break-even is $103. This is better than a naked call if you do not expect much above $110.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid if you expect explosive upside far beyond the short strike, because the short call caps profits. Also avoid if the debit is too large relative to the spread width.
strategy_playbook.management: Consider closing when the spread reaches 70-90% of max value. Waiting for the last dollars can expose you to reversal near expiration.
strategy_playbook.risks: Upside capped at short strike. A slow or small move can still lose if the debit is not overcome.

strategy_playbook.name: Covered call
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Fits a neutral to mildly bullish market where the stock may grind higher or stay range-bound, IV is high enough to pay worthwhile premium, and you are willing to sell shares at the call strike.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use when you already own shares and want income, or when you would be satisfied exiting the stock at a higher price. The short call should be at a strike where assignment would be acceptable.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: you own 100 shares at $100. Sell the 110 call for $3. If the stock stays below $110, you keep $300. If assigned at $110, your outcome is roughly $10 stock gain plus $3 premium, or $1,300 before fees. If the stock rallies to $125, you still likely sell at $110 and miss upside above the strike.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid tight covered calls in strong risk-on trends when you do not want to cap upside. Avoid if you would be upset selling shares at the strike.
strategy_playbook.management: If stock approaches the short strike, decide whether assignment is acceptable. Roll only if the new strike, credit/debit, and added time improve the plan.
strategy_playbook.risks: Stock can fall more than premium collected. Upside is capped and assignment can occur, especially around dividends.

strategy_playbook.name: Cash-secured put
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Fits a neutral to mildly bullish market where you are willing to own the stock lower, support is nearby, and IV is rich enough to compensate you for assignment risk.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use when you want to get paid while waiting for a lower entry. The strike should be a price where you genuinely want to own shares.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: stock is at $100 and you would like to buy at $95. Sell the 95 put for $2.50. If the stock stays above $95, you keep $250. If assigned, your effective entry is $92.50 before fees. If the stock falls to $75, you still own or are obligated near $92.50, so risk remains large.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid on stocks you do not want to own, before unknown binary events, or when the premium is tiny compared with downside risk.
strategy_playbook.management: Consider buying back the put after capturing most of the premium. If the stock breaks support, reassess whether you still want assignment.
strategy_playbook.risks: Assignment into a falling stock. Effective entry can still be far above market price after a sharp decline.

strategy_playbook.name: Long put
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Fits bearish or risk-off conditions when trend is weakening, support is breaking, VIX is not already extremely inflated, and you want defined-risk downside exposure.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use when you expect a meaningful decline within the option's life and want max loss limited to premium. It can also be used as a directional hedge when you do not own the stock.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: stock breaks support at $100 and you expect a move to $90. Buy the 100 put for $4. Break-even at expiration is $96. If the stock falls to $88, the put is worth $12 and gross profit is $8 per share. If the stock drifts sideways, theta can erode the premium.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid chasing puts after IV has already exploded unless you expect further downside greater than the premium priced in.
strategy_playbook.management: Take partial or full profits when the expected downside move happens. If price recovers above the invalidation level, close rather than waiting for expiration.
strategy_playbook.risks: Timing and IV crush after events. A correct bearish view can still lose if the decline is too slow or IV falls.

strategy_playbook.name: Bear put spread
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Fits bearish markets where you expect downside toward a specific target but want to reduce the cost of buying a put, especially when IV is moderate or high.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use when you have a downside target. Buy a put near current price or resistance breakdown area, and sell a lower put near the target zone. This lowers cost but caps profit.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: stock is at $100 and you expect $90. Buy the 100 put for $5 and sell the 90 put for $2. Net debit is $3. Max value is $10, so max profit is $7. Break-even is $97. If stock falls to $90 or lower at expiration, the spread can reach max value.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid if you expect a crash far beyond the short put, because profit is capped. Avoid if the debit is too large relative to spread width.
strategy_playbook.management: Close when the spread reaches most of max value or if the bearish thesis fails. Do not wait for max profit if price reaches target early.
strategy_playbook.risks: Profit capped at spread width. A slow decline may not overcome the debit before expiration.

strategy_playbook.name: Iron condor
strategy_playbook.structure: Bull put spread + bear call spread
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Fits neutral or range-bound markets where price is likely to stay between support and resistance and IV is elevated enough to pay a worthwhile credit.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use when you expect limited movement and want defined-risk premium selling. The short strikes should be outside the expected range and beyond key support/resistance zones.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: stock is at $100, support is near $92, resistance near $108, and IV is elevated. Sell the 90/85 put spread and 110/115 call spread for a total $2 credit. Max profit is $200. If both spreads are $5 wide, max loss is $300. Profit zone is between the short strikes at expiration.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid before events that can move price outside the range unless the credit is large enough and max loss is acceptable. Avoid in strong trends.
strategy_playbook.management: Many traders close at 50-75% of max profit. If one side is tested, close or adjust based on the original range thesis.
strategy_playbook.risks: Gap moves outside long strikes. Loss can be larger than credit received.

strategy_playbook.name: Long straddle
strategy_playbook.structure: Buy call and put same strike
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Fits event-driven markets when direction is unclear but you expect a move larger than the option market is pricing. Best when IV is low or fair before the event, not already extremely inflated.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use when the move matters more than direction. The combined premium is the hurdle. The stock must move far enough, or IV must rise after entry, to overcome the cost of both options.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: stock is at $100. Buy the 100 call for $4 and the 100 put for $4. Total cost is $8. Upper break-even is $108 and lower break-even is $92. If earnings move the stock to $115, the structure can profit. If the stock moves only to $104 and IV crushes, the straddle may lose.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid when the expected move is already fully priced or IV is extremely high before the event.
strategy_playbook.management: Some traders close before the event if IV expansion creates a profit. If holding through the event, size for the possibility of losing most of the premium.
strategy_playbook.risks: Theta and post-event IV crush can hurt both legs. Needs a large move, not just volatility in headlines.

strategy_playbook.name: Protective put
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Fits cautious long markets where you still want to hold shares but risk-off conditions, earnings, or macro events could create downside.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use when the main goal is protecting an existing stock position. The put strike should match the drawdown you can tolerate.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: own 100 shares at $100 and buy a 95 put for $3. If stock falls to $80, the put gains value below $95 and reduces the drawdown. If stock rallies, you keep upside but the $300 premium reduces net return.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid if the protection is too expensive relative to the risk period, or if simply reducing shares would be cleaner.
strategy_playbook.management: If the stock drops, decide whether to monetize the put, keep protection, or exit shares. If risk passes, consider closing the put to recover remaining value.
strategy_playbook.risks: Premium reduces net returns. Far OTM puts may not protect until after a large loss.

strategy_playbook.name: Collar
strategy_playbook.structure: Long stock, long put, short call
strategy_playbook.market_setup: Fits cautious long or risk-off transition markets where you own stock, want a defined downside floor, and are willing to cap upside to reduce hedge cost.
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Use after gains, before uncertain events, or when you want to keep shares but define a range of outcomes. The put provides the floor; the call helps finance it.
strategy_playbook.example: Example: own stock at $100. Buy a 95 put for $3 and sell a 110 call for $2. Net hedge cost is $1. Downside is cushioned below $95, but upside is capped near $110. This can protect gains while keeping some upside.
strategy_playbook.avoid_when: Avoid if you are strongly bullish and would regret selling shares at the call strike. Avoid if the call credit is too small to justify the upside cap.
strategy_playbook.management: If price approaches the call strike, decide whether to accept assignment or roll. If price falls, the put is working; decide whether to keep protection or reduce shares.
strategy_playbook.risks: Upside capped by short call. Assignment risk exists on the short call, especially around dividends.

checklists.title: Daily regime check
checklists.summary: Run this at the start of the session before choosing any structure. It answers whether the market is risk-on, neutral, risk-off, or event-driven.
checklists.when_to_use: Use every trading day, before Market regime guide deep reading if you already know the basics, and always before opening new risk.

items.question: Is VIX rising, falling, or stable?
items.why_it_matters: VIX direction helps classify whether fear is entering or leaving the market. Rising VIX often favors hedges, smaller size, and defined-risk structures. Falling VIX often favors directional long exposure.
items.example: Example: VIX rises from 15 to 19 while indexes sell off. That supports a more defensive posture: smaller bullish bets, more hedging, or bearish structures. VIX falling from 22 to 17 during a rally supports risk-on bullish setups.
items.red_flag: If VIX is spiking and you are adding aggressive bullish premium-selling trades without a hedge, pause.

items.question: Are more stocks advancing than declining?
items.why_it_matters: Breadth tells you whether the move is broad or narrow. A rally led by only a few names is weaker than broad participation.
items.example: Example: SPY is flat, but advance/decline is strongly positive and small caps participate. That can still be risk-on stock selection. If indexes rise but breadth is poor, breakouts may fail more often.
items.red_flag: If your bullish trade depends on broad market strength but breadth is weak, reduce size or wait.

items.question: Is growth or defensives leading?
items.why_it_matters: Sector leadership reveals whether investors are reaching for upside or hiding in safety.
items.example: Example: technology and consumer discretionary lead while utilities and staples lag. That fits risk-on. If defensives lead while growth lags, be careful with aggressive call buying even if one chart looks good.
items.red_flag: Do not buy breakout calls in a growth name if the sector is lagging badly unless the thesis is company-specific.

items.question: Are bad headlines ignored or punished?
items.why_it_matters: This is a market character test. Bad news ignored often means risk-on. Bad news punished quickly often means risk-off.
items.example: Example: a hot inflation print hits and the index dips 0.3% then recovers. Bad news is being ignored. Another day, a mild guidance cut sends a stock down 8%. The market is punishing weakness.
items.red_flag: If bad news is being punished broadly, avoid oversized dip-buying without a hedge.

items.question: Is my symbol's IV above or below its recent average?
items.why_it_matters: Relative IV helps decide whether to buy premium, sell premium, or use spreads. High IV makes long options expensive. Low IV makes long options cheaper but offers less credit for sellers.
items.example: Example: stock IV rank is 75 and earnings are not yet priced in a week away. Long calls are expensive. A bull call spread or waiting may be better. If IV rank is 20 in a risk-on breakout, long calls may be more efficient.
items.red_flag: If IV is expensive and you still want directional exposure, spreads or stock may be better than naked long options.

checklists.title: Pre-trade options checklist
checklists.summary: Use after Market regime guide and Strategy playbook. This is the final gate before sending an order.
checklists.when_to_use: Use before every new options trade, spread, hedge, or roll. If any answer is vague, revise the trade or skip it.

items.question: What regime am I in (risk-on, neutral, risk-off, event-driven)?
items.why_it_matters: The same bullish idea can be smart in risk-on and poor in risk-off. Regime determines whether you should be aggressive, neutral, or defensive.
items.example: Example: bullish on a stock in risk-on with VIX falling -> compare stock, long call, or bull call spread. Same bullish idea in risk-off -> smaller size, protective put, or wait.
items.red_flag: If you cannot name the regime, do not trade yet.

items.question: Is IV cheap, fair, expensive, or event-driven for this symbol?
items.why_it_matters: IV affects both structure choice and required move. Expensive IV hurts buyers. Cheap IV offers less edge for sellers unless range behavior is strong.
items.example: Example: IV rank 80 before earnings. Buying a straddle may face IV crush. Selling a wide iron condor may collect rich premium but has gap risk. IV rank 25 during a clean breakout may favor long calls or debit spreads.
items.red_flag: If IV is expensive and your plan is to buy ATM options without a strong catalyst, reconsider.

items.question: What is my maximum loss in dollars and percent of account?
items.why_it_matters: Defined risk is only real after converting contracts into dollars. This prevents oversizing.
items.example: Example: 5 bull call spreads at $2.50 debit risk $1,250 total. On a $30,000 account that is 4.2%. If that is within your rule, proceed. If it is 12%, reduce contracts.
items.red_flag: If max loss is uncomfortable or uncalculated, size down or skip.

items.question: What price or date proves me wrong?
items.why_it_matters: Invalidation turns an opinion into a plan. Options also need a time stop because theta can hurt without a price move.
items.example: Example: buy a breakout call after $100 resistance break. Invalidation is daily close back below $100. Time stop: exit if no follow-through within 5 sessions.
items.red_flag: If invalidation is unclear, the trade is not ready.

items.question: What happens if the stock does not move?
items.why_it_matters: Many option losses come from no movement, not from being wrong on direction. Theta and IV changes matter.
items.example: Example: buy a 45 DTE call for $4. If stock stays near unchanged for three weeks, the call may fall to $2 even without a bearish move. A covered call or credit spread may have behaved better in that environment.
items.red_flag: If the trade only works with a fast move and you have no catalyst, avoid long premium.

items.question: Are bid/ask spreads acceptable?
items.why_it_matters: Wide spreads increase true cost and make exits harder.
items.example: Example: option is $1.00 x $1.40. Round-trip slippage can be $0.40 per share, or $40 per contract. On a $200 trade that is material. Prefer strikes with tighter markets.
items.red_flag: If spread is more than about 10-15% of the option price, be very cautious.

items.question: Does expiration match my catalyst timeline?
items.why_it_matters: Too little time creates theta pressure. Too much time costs more premium than needed.
items.example: Example: earnings in 12 days. A 7 DTE call may decay too fast even if direction is right. A 60 DTE call may pay for more time than needed. Choose expiration around the event plus a small buffer.
items.red_flag: If expiration does not match the thesis timeline, adjust or skip.

items.question: Have I modeled the trade in the payoff simulator?
items.why_it_matters: Modeling forces you to see break-even, max loss, and scenario outcomes before capital is committed.
items.example: Example: before selling an iron condor, model a flat market, a 5% up move, and a 5% down move. If one gap scenario exceeds your comfort, reduce size or widen strikes.
items.red_flag: If you have not modeled max loss and break-even, do not send the order.

checklists.title: Covered call management
checklists.summary: Use when you already own shares and are managing an existing or planned covered call.
checklists.when_to_use: Use before opening a new covered call, when price approaches the strike, before expiration, and before rolling.

items.question: Is IV still high enough to justify a new sale?
items.why_it_matters: Covered calls are most attractive when premium is meaningful relative to the risk of capping upside.
items.example: Example: stock at $100, 30 DTE 105 call pays $1.50 with elevated IV. That may be worthwhile if you would sell at $105. If the same call pays $0.35 with low IV, the income may not justify capping upside.
items.red_flag: If premium is tiny and trend is strongly bullish, selling a call may be a bad tradeoff.

items.question: Is the stock near resistance?
items.why_it_matters: Selling a call near resistance can align with a level where you are willing to exit shares.
items.example: Example: stock rallies into $110 resistance and you own from $100. Selling the 110 call may match your plan to exit there. Selling a 105 call far below resistance may cap the stock too early.
items.red_flag: If strike is inside obvious upside target zone and you still want the shares, do not sell that strike.

items.question: If price exceeds strike, will I roll, accept assignment, or close?
items.why_it_matters: You should know the answer before price gets there. Otherwise decisions become emotional.
items.example: Example: short 110 call with stock at $109. Plan: if stock closes above $110 and you are happy selling, accept assignment. If you want to keep shares, roll up and out only if the roll improves the plan after fees.
items.red_flag: If you have no assignment/roll plan, pause before price crosses the strike.

items.question: Did I calculate roll credit/debit before acting?
items.why_it_matters: Rolling is not free alpha. A roll that costs too much debit can erase prior premium collected.
items.example: Example: buy back the 110 call for $2.00 and sell the 115 call next month for $1.20. Net debit is $0.80. That may be acceptable if you want more upside room. If net debit is $2.50, the roll may be too expensive.
items.red_flag: If roll math is worse than simply letting shares go or closing the call, do not roll blindly.
